title: Choose Northline's visual world
question: Which direction should carry this reusable contractor demo? Choose one, steer the hand, or take the familiar category standard.

options.label: The Daily Build Log
options.lineage: jobsite progress boards, foreman logs, and dated inspection marks
options.thesis: The website behaves like a live build record: phases are visible, details are marked, and the next action is never buried.
options.viewport: A panoramic finished home is crossed by one slim progress rail; the headline, project phase, and estimate action read as one field note.
options.risk: Can feel overly operational unless the home photography and quiet spacing preserve warmth.

raised.raise: One decisive project image owns the opening viewport.
Every annotation aligns to an auditable modular grid.
The visitor path advances in a measured sequence from vision to plan to build.
Warm material light offsets the technical project language.
Project phase and form state stay legible without relying on color alone.

options.label: The Architect's Field Book
options.lineage: architectural notebooks, measured drawings, and material callouts
options.thesis: A calm, tactile field book turns each service and project into a considered drawing with a human note beside it.
options.viewport: An asymmetric plan-sheet composition pairs a large home photograph with an oversized promise and hand-drawn project callouts.
options.risk: This is the most familiar premium direction and may lean closer to an architecture studio than a working contractor.

options.label: Vertical Project Stories
options.thesis: Each project fills the screen while a compact action rail turns browsing into an estimate conversation.
options.viewport: One finished kitchen fills the viewport, with service caption low left and estimate controls stacked at right.
options.case: The work is instantly legible and memorable, but a feed makes process and trust information harder to scan.
options.risk: It can feel like social media instead of a dependable local service business.

options.label: The Warm Workshop
options.thesis: Services unfold like lit workshop forms, making craftsmanship feel warm, patient, and distinctly human.
options.viewport: A softly lit interior rises from a paper-toned ground while the estimate action reads like a maker's seal.
options.case: It leads on warmth and craft identification, but says less about the contractor's process and reliability.
options.risk: The quiet atmosphere may undersell the scale and rigor of general contracting.

options.label: Signal Grid
options.thesis: Every service becomes a connected signal on a strict construction grid.
options.viewport: A black-and-paper grid routes the visitor from project type to estimate.
options.case: The mechanics are clear, but homeowners would not immediately identify it with trusted residential work.
options.kept: Relentless alignment discipline and explicit active states.
options.risk: Feels industrial and abstract for a residential contractor.

options.label: The Axial Walk
options.lineage: Versailles garden axes and concealed rooms
options.thesis: The page reveals a project in measured vistas from first idea to finished room.
options.viewport: A symmetrical project vista leads the eye through service, process, and contact thresholds.
options.case: The sequence is elegant, but the cultural signal is too distant from a working general contractor.
options.kept: A choreographed visitor path with deliberate reveals.
options.risk: Can become ceremonial when the job is practical trust-building.

options.label: The Phase Schedule
options.thesis: Numbered construction lanes make every project phase and request state explicit.
options.viewport: An amber schedule routes a homeowner from scope to project phase to estimate.
options.case: It excels at state clarity but reads like a control room rather than a welcoming home service.
options.kept: States remain legible through line patterns, labels, and shape rather than color alone.
options.risk: The technical language could alienate residential visitors.

options.label: The Measured Counter
options.thesis: Visible quantities turn the contractor's work into a precise instrument panel.
options.viewport: A dark instrument panel frames project quantities and the estimate action.
options.case: Without verified metrics, the counter mechanism has no honest content to carry.
options.kept: Motion appears only where a meaningful project state changes.
options.risk: It depends on proof data this fictional demo does not have.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A polished local contractor site with a photo hero, service cards, project gallery, and estimate form.
canonCard.viewport: A navigation bar sits above a split photo-and-copy hero with a large estimate button.
canonCard.risk: Immediately understandable, but intentionally difficult to distinguish from other contractor templates.
